title: Act III, Scene V
focus: Hecate and the machinery of fate

teacherSummary.text: Hecate angrily scolds the Witches, 'beldams' who are 'saucy and overbold,' for trading with Macbeth in riddles without her, for a 'wayward son' who loves for his own ends. She orders them to meet her at the pit of Acheron in the morning, where Macbeth will come to know his destiny, and plans illusions that will draw him on to his confusion. 'Security is mortals' chiefest enemy.'

symbolsAndMotifs.name: the prophecies
symbolsAndMotifs.explanation: The witches' riddling prophecies (Birnam Wood, no man of woman born) feed Macbeth's false confidence and then destroy it. In this scene: “scorn death, and bear / He hopes ’bove wisdom, grace and fear: / And you all know, security / Is mortals’ chiefest enemy. Music and” (Act III, Scene V, Hecate (speech 2)).

symbolsAndMotifs.name: darkness and light
symbolsAndMotifs.explanation: Night and darkness hide crimes; the Macbeths call on darkness to cover their deeds, and putting out a light marks murder. In this scene: “and every thing beside. / I am for the air; this night I’ll spend / Unto a dismal and a fatal end: / Great business” (Act III, Scene V, Hecate (speech 2)).

followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: A defensible line of argument: Hecate's plan is to destroy Macbeth through his own overconfidence. Useful evidence: “He shall spurn fate, scorn death, and bear” (Act III, Scene V, Hecate (speech 2)): Her plan for Macbeth: confidence will make him careless. Theme link: Hecate says security is "mortals' chiefest enemy." Credit any position that is supported by quotation and reasoning; push one-sided answers to address the strongest counterpoint.

middleSchool.note: Excerpt-based: read the passage aloud first; use the scaffolds; accept partial answers and build with probes.

hsFreshman.note: Use the scaffolds for literal and inferential items; require one quotation for every inferential answer.

hsSophomore.note: Require a quotation and an explanation; push evaluative answers to address a counterclaim.

hsJunior.note: Emphasize structure and ambiguity; students should name where the text leaves matters open.

hsSenior.note: Weigh competing interpretations; students should defend the stronger reading.

ap.note: Treat each evaluative item as a thesis rehearsal: defensible claim, purposeful evidence, commentary on choices.

collegeFreshman.note: Add the extension: connect answers to historical context and one secondary perspective.

collegeSophomore.note: Use the extensions: genre and period conventions, and a published critic.

collegeJunior.note: Use the extensions: name a critical method and test it against the passage.

collegeSenior.note: Use the extensions: connect the scene to the whole work and the scholarship.

graduate.note: Use the extensions: position answers in a critical conversation and the textual history.
